newsitem.title: ALBANIA: Albania mission on track, mediator Vranitzky says.
newsitem.headline: Albania mission on track, mediator Vranitzky says.

text.p: Franz Vranitzky, international mediator for volatile Albania, said on Wednesday a multinational security mission was on the right track although it had no mandate at present to disarm civilians.

Vranitzky, envoy of the Organisation of Security and Cooperation in Europe (OSCE), met Prime Minister Bashkim Fino at the start of his third trip to Albania since an armed uprising brought the nation to the brink of collapse.
He was also planning to meet President Sali Berisha as well as officials from local authorities in rebel-held parts of the country during the two-day visit.

But Vranitzky immediately ran into criticism from the newspaper of Berisha's Democratic Party and the independent daily Albania said he was "walking on a minefield" because of his plans to contact rebels in the south who want Berisha to quit.
Arriving at Tirana airport, Vranitzky said he was pleased with the start of Operation Alba, an eight-nation security mission that aims to protect humanitarian aid convoys.
"It's always bad to draw conclusions when a mission starts, but I have the feeling that we are on the right track so far with our mission," Vranitzky told reporters.
"Today, our purpose is to enforce it and continue it," he added.
Vranitzky was speaking one day after nearly 1,200 troops arrived by air and sea to launch a U.N.-backed security mission to protect relief deliveries to the chaotic Balkan state.
Vranitzky said the 6,000-strong eight-nation force had no mandate to disarm Albanians who seized weapons from army depots during weeks of banditry. Nearly 300 people have been killed.
"We have the mandate that the U.N. gave us. We can't change it in the short time," he said.
"We are working together with the Albanians. We will tell the Albanians we can't solve their problems but that we are going to help them to help themselves.

The Democratic Party newspaper, Rilindja Demokratike, said Vranitzky's mission may be compromised by the fact that on his last trip in March, he met anti-Berisha rebel leaders from the southern town of Vlore but not the president himself.
"Such positions may compromise the neutrality of Vranitzky's mission in Albania and endanger his success -- something we don't want," the paper said in an editorial.
Fino's Socialist party was in opposition before forming an all-party emergency government with Berisha's Democatic party last month.
Vranitzky, chancellor of Austria until January, was expected to meet Berisha and other political leaders later on Wednesday.
On Thursday, he is scheduled to fly by helicopter to Vlore and the northern town of Shkoder.
Vlore is a southern port town where a violent uprising after the collapse of fraudulent savings schemes began in February, and has been controlled by a rebel committee ever since.

"The minefield he is walking on now might blow up not only his mission but also the future of peace in Albania," the independent Albania newspaper said in a front-page editorial, referring to Vranitzky's contacts with the rebels.

Although Shkoder is still in government hands, renewed violence has flared in recent days and local authorities have urged the interior ministry to send special protection forces. The government has already done so in some southern towns.
